entries.name: Qhapaq Ñan (Andean Road System)
entries.era: c. 1400-1533 CE, built mostly in the 15th century on pre-Inca foundations
entries.purpose: imperial army, chasqui courier and trade artery across Tawantinsuyu
layout: four main strands radiate from Cusco, one per suyo, tied by coastal and sierra longitudinal roads
steps wherever the grade defeats wheeled or hoofed travel
retaining walls and stepped ledges where the road crosses cliffs
entries.found: along the Andes from southern Colombia through Ecuador, Peru and Bolivia to northwestern Argentina and central Chile
entries.notes: UNESCO World Heritage (2014); over 30,000 km by UNESCO's count, some estimates say 40,000. Chasqui relay runners carried messages the length of the empire, roughly 240 km a day.

entries.name: Silk Road
entries.purpose: overland exchange of silk, horses, glass, spices, ideas and religions between China and the Mediterranean
parts: chain of oasis cities (Chang'an, Samarkand, Merv, Palmyra)
northern steppe and southern Taklamakan rim branches
layout: not one road but a lattice; caravans hopped from oasis to oasis
northern branch skirted the Tien Shan and Altai; southern branch ringed the Taklamakan desert
traffic faded as Indian Ocean shipping grew after the 1400s
entries.found: from the Chinese capital west through Central Asia to the Levant and the Mediterranean
entries.notes: Opened after Zhang Qian's mission to the Yuezhi (139 BCE); Marco Polo travelled it c. 1271-1295. Silk bought in Chang'an sold at Antioch for many times its purchase price.

entries.name: Tōkaidō (Eastern Sea Route)
entries.purpose: shogunate artery between Edo and Kyoto; daimyo alternate-attendance (sankin-kōtai) processions travelled it
parts: river ferries and bridges at the major crossings
tea houses, inns, horse and palanquin hire
layout: hugged the Pacific side of Honshū, longer and gentler than the mountain Nakasendō
post towns spaced a day's walk apart with inns licensed by the shogunate
traffic ranked by status: daimyo retinues, officials, pilgrims, merchants
entries.found: from Edo (Tokyo) southwest along the coast to the capital (Kyoto)
entries.notes: Hiroshige's 1832 woodblock series The Fifty-three Stations of the Tōkaidō made the road famous worldwide. It is the ancestor of the modern Tōmei Expressway and the Tokaido Shinkansen corridor.

entries.name: Via Egnatia
entries.era: c. 146 BCE onward; used into the Byzantine period
entries.purpose: Roman strategic road from the Adriatic to Byzantium; moved legions, mail and goods
layout: from Dyrrhachium and Apollonia across the Balkans via Thessalonica to Byzantium
crossed the Pindus and other ranges in engineered passes
dead-straight between stations where the ground allowed
entries.found: modern Albania, North Macedonia, Greece, and European Turkey
entries.notes: About 1,120 km. St Paul travelled it on his missionary journeys (Acts 16-17); the modern Egnatia Odos motorway retraces it.

entries.name: Persian Royal Road
entries.purpose: imperial courier and army road from Sardis (Lydia) to Susa
parts: fresh horses and riders at every station
guarded ferries over the great rivers
layout: from Sardis through Phrygia and the Anatolian plateau, along the upper Euphrates, across the Zagros to Susa
stations a fast day apart for royal mounted couriers
inspected and garrisoned as imperial infrastructure
entries.found: western Anatolia to Khuzistan (modern Turkey, Syria, Iraq, Iran)
entries.notes: Herodotus 5.52-53 and 8.98: 111 royal posting stations; the angareion (post) was the fastest state service of antiquity. The US Post Office bears his 'neither snow nor rain nor heat nor gloom of night' line.

entries.name: Great Ocean Road
entries.purpose: touring and timber-access road; Depression-era employment scheme for returned servicemen
parts: cliff-perched carriageway over the Southern Ocean
memorial arches at the eastern and western ends
layout: between Torquay and Allansford, 243 km along the Surf Coast and the Otway fringe
benched into sea cliffs, on rock fill over gullies
tight, slow corners; speeds well below highway norms
entries.found: Victoria's southwestern coast, Australia
entries.notes: Roughly 3,000 returned servicemen built it after the First World War; the eastern terminus at Torquay holds a memorial arch.

entries.name: Route 66 (Will Rogers Highway)
entries.purpose: first all-weather Chicago-Los Angeles corridor; main artery of Depression-era westward migration
parts: long river spans (e.g., over the Mississippi)
layout: from Chicago to Santa Monica through St. Louis, Oklahoma City, Amarillo and Flagstaff
progressively bypassed by the Interstate system 1956-1984
largely survives as state and local roads; signposted in places
entries.found: Illinois, Missouri, Kansas, Oklahoma, Texas, New Mexico, Arizona, California
entries.notes: 2,448 miles (3,940 km). John Steinbeck called it 'the Mother Road' in The Grapes of Wrath (1939); the shield retired in 1985.

entries.name: US Interstate Highway System
materials: steel girder and prestressed concrete bridges
entries.purpose: national defense and interstate commerce; 90% federally funded limited-access freeways
layout: grid of even/odd numbered routes (north-south odd, east-west even), with spurs around cities
access only via interchanges; no at-grade crossings
numbering encodes direction and region
entries.found: all 50 states (Alaska and Hawaii have in-state freeway networks)
entries.notes: About 77,000 km; the largest public works programme in US history, signed by President Eisenhower, who admired the German autobahns seen in 1945.

entries.name: Autobahn (Reichsautobahn)
entries.era: 1932 first segment Köln-Bonn; greatly expanded 1933-1945; still expanding
entries.purpose: fast motor road linking Germany's industrial heartland; military and propaganda symbol
parts: no general speed limit on many sections
layout: radiating and linking rings from the Rhine, the Ruhr and Berlin
designed for uninterrupted high-speed running, unlike earlier AVUS racing track
widened and modernized continuously since 1945
entries.found: throughout Germany, densest west of the Elbe
entries.notes: Around 13,000 km; grew from Weimar-era planning, not a Nazi invention, but was built as showpiece infrastructure with forced labour.

entries.name: Pan-American Highway
entries.purpose: continental road network linking Alaska to Patagonia
parts: linked national highways from Anchorage to Ushuaia
layout: several roughly parallel routes branch and rejoin across the Americas
broken by the Darién Gap (Panama-Colombia), about 160 km of impassable jungle deliberately left unbuilt
passes over the Andes connect coastal and sierra branches
entries.found: North, Central and South America
entries.notes: About 30,000 km, the longest road network on Earth; the unfinished Darién Gap keeps the ends from ever meeting.

entries.name: Grossglockner High Alpine Road
entries.purpose: tourist drive over the Hohe Tauern; jobs for Depression-era Austria
layout: between Bruck an der Glocknerstraße and Heiligenblut, 48 km
climbs through pine then bare rock and ice to a pass crest
open roughly May to October; toll road
entries.found: Salzburg and Carinthia, Austria
entries.notes: Europe's most famous mountain toll road; engineering masterpiece of interwar Austria. Highest point Hochtor at 2,504 m.

entries.name: Macadam road
materials: broken angular stone, compacted in layers
entries.purpose: cheap, durable road without deep foundations; the default roadbed of the 19th century
parts: compacted 150 mm layers of broken stone
layout: raised, well-drained camber sheds water instead of relying on deep foundations
20 mm and smaller aggregate on top, bound by stone dust
a tar-bound version, tarmac (1901), gave the modern surface
entries.found: every developed country from the 1820s onward
entries.notes: John Loudon McAdam, 1820s Scotland. His insight was drainage, not strength: a thin, well-cambered, stone-dust layer, rolled by traffic, outlasted thick foundations.

entries.name: Corduroy road
entries.era: antiquity to the 20th century (pioneer and military)
entries.purpose: cross swamp, muskeg and bog without wheeled vehicles sinking
parts: parallel rows of logs across the track
layout: logs laid side by side at right angles to the line of travel
wheels ride log-end to log-end; hooves stay out of the mud
rots in a few years; kept up by constant replacement
entries.found: colonial and Civil War supply roads, Canadian muskeg, Siberian taiga
entries.notes: The sound alone announced a corduroy road; carts rattled across it and riders hated it. Standard in swamp crossings into the early 20th century.

entries.name: Drove road
entries.era: medieval to 19th century (Spain's cañadas still law)
entries.purpose: walk livestock hundreds of kilometres to market; cattle graze the verges en route
parts: wide grassy corridor (up to 36 m or more)
inns and smithies at the termini
layout: broad straight corridors along parish and manor boundaries
wide enough that hundreds of head could move and feed without trampling crops
deepened by hoofs over centuries into hollowed-out lanes
entries.found: Britain (Welsh drove roads to the Midlands and London) and Iberia (cañadas reales)
entries.notes: Hoof-hollows and wide green hedges still mark them; Spain's cañadas reales remain protected in law as ancient public rights of way.

entries.name: Holloway (sunken lane)
entries.purpose: a way worn deep by traffic and rain; the sunken counterpart to a drove road
parts: sunken track 1-5 m below the fields
layout: formed by walkers, carts and ploughs plus rain runoff
follows the oldest available line, often prehistoric or Roman
tunnel-like enclosure makes a distinct microclimate
entries.found: southern England, especially Wiltshire, Dorset and the Weald
entries.notes: Centuries of hooves, wheels and rain cut them down; some retain prehistoric alignments. Hedged holloways shelter birds and rare ferns.

entries.name: Via Salaria (Salt Road)
entries.purpose: move salt from the Adriatic to Rome
layout: from the Adriatic (Picenum) through the Sabine hills to Rome
over the Apennine passes into the Tiber valley
lined with salt stores at regular intervals
entries.found: central Italy, from the Adriatic coast to Rome
entries.notes: Salt was Rome's ration and preservative; the road's name survives in 'salary' (salarium, money for salt). One of Rome's oldest highways.

entries.name: Incense Route
entries.purpose: move frankincense and myrrh from South Arabia to the Mediterranean
parts: caravan trains of thousands of camels
layout: from southern Arabia up the Hejaz and across the Negev to Gaza
hopped from well to well; every caravan depended on stored water
terminated at the Mediterranean for onward shipment
entries.found: Gaza to the Arabian Peninsula, through the Negev and the Sinai
entries.notes: UNESCO World Heritage (2005) for the Negev desert cities. Frankincense was worth its weight in silver in Roman markets.

entries.name: Amber Road
entries.purpose: carry Baltic amber to the Mediterranean
parts: tolls and sorting in Pannonia and Aquileia
layout: from the Samland coast (modern Kaliningrad/Poland) south through Central Europe to the Po valley
followed rivers and low passes, avoiding the Alpine crest where possible
goods moved in barrels and cakes of raw amber, sorted at Aquileia
entries.found: from the Baltic coast through Central Europe to northern Italy
entries.notes: The Romans imported amber in bulk; Pliny complained a modest amber statue cost more than a healthy slave.

entries.name: Golden Gate Bridge
entries.purpose: road crossing of the Golden Gate strait between San Francisco and Marin County
parts: two Art Deco towers, 227 m above water
six traffic lanes and a pedestrian walkway
layout: spans the strait at a single stretch; no piers in the shipping channel
towers on concrete fender piers sunk to bedrock
painted International Orange for visibility in fog
entries.found: San Francisco, California, USA (Golden Gate strait)
entries.notes: Chief engineer Joseph Strauss; 11 men died building it. Opened 27 May 1937. Painted endlessly; the US maintains the coat continuously.

entries.name: Brooklyn Bridge
entries.purpose: first fixed road crossing of the East River between Manhattan and Brooklyn
parts: hybrid cable-stayed and suspension main span 486 m
layout: crosses from New York City Hall area to Brooklyn Heights
the promenade runs above the carriageways on diagonal stays
first day: about 1,800 vehicles and 150,000 people
entries.found: New York City, USA (East River)
entries.notes: Designed by John A. Roebling, finished by his son Washington and daughter-in-law Emily Warren Roebling after John died in 1869. Opened 24 May 1883.

entries.name: Sydney Harbour Bridge
entries.purpose: road, rail, cycle and pedestrian link across Port Jackson
parts: four granite-faced pylons, decorative, not load-bearing
eight traffic lanes and two rail tracks
layout: arch rib springs from cliff-sited foundations; the deck hangs from it on steel hangers
deck hung from the arch; approaches on reinforced concrete viaducts
opened 19 March 1932; de Groot sabotaged the opening by cutting the ribbon on horseback
entries.found: Port Jackson, Sydney, Australia
entries.notes: Nicknamed 'the Coathanger'. The pylons are pure decoration; the arch does all the work. Climb operator BridgeClimb runs trips over the arch daily since 1998.

entries.name: Akashi Kaikyō Bridge
materials: steel truss and box girder deck
entries.purpose: road crossing of the Akashi Strait (Honshū to Awaji Island)
layout: spans the strait between Kobe and Awaji Island; no piers in the sea channel
towers founded on caissons sunk to the seabed
withstood the 1995 Great Hanshin earthquake mid-construction; the span grew 1 m
entries.found: Akashi Strait, Hyōgo Prefecture, Japan
entries.notes: Longest suspension span in the world from 1998 until the 1915 Çanakkale Bridge opened in 2022 (2,023 m). Endured the Kobe quake without damage.

entries.name: Forth Bridge (rail)
entries.purpose: rail crossing of the Firth of Forth for heavy trains
parts: two main cantilever spans of 521 m
layout: from South Queensferry to North Queensferry
parallel lines for two tracks
paint crew never fully finishes; painting is said never to end
entries.found: Firth of Forth near Queensferry, Scotland
entries.notes: Britain's first great steel bridge; world's longest cantilever span until 1919 (Québec Bridge). UNESCO World Heritage (2015). Still carries freight and passenger trains.

entries.name: Old London Bridge (medieval)
entries.purpose: road crossing of the Thames combining bridge, shop street and gate; rents funded maintenance
parts: two rows of houses and shops up to five storeys
southern stone gate with pikes for traitors' heads
layout: about 926 feet (282 m) long
houses up to five storeys over the piers, projecting on hammer beams
roadway only about 4.5-6 m wide; house shops fronted it
starlings caused a 1.8 m water-level difference; rapids under the central arch
entries.found: the River Thames between the City of London and Southwark
entries.notes: Up to 140 houses by the late 14th century; a 1.8 m drop across the starlings drowned many before the 1757-1759 Great Arch. Demolished 1831.

entries.name: Ponte Vecchio
entries.era: 1345 to now (replacing earlier wooden bridges on the same site)
entries.purpose: road crossing of the Arno; shop rents paid for upkeep
parts: rows of shops (botteghe) cantilevered over both sides
Vasari Corridor running above the deck (1565)
layout: spans the Arno at its narrowest point
shops projecting over both sides, back jetties added in the 17th century
the only Florence bridge spared by the retreating German army in August 1944
entries.found: Florence, Italy (Via Por Santa Maria to Via de' Guicciardini)
entries.notes: Butchers evicted in 1565 by ducal decree; goldsmiths since. Rebuilt 1345 after the 1333 flood; the only Arno bridge not destroyed in 1944.

entries.name: Rialto Bridge (Ponte di Rialto)
entries.era: 1591 (current stone bridge; wooden bridges from c. 1173)
entries.purpose: main foot crossing of the Grand Canal and the commercial centre of Venice
parts: single stone arch span of 28.8 m
two rows of 24 shops on the deck
three walkways separated by the shops
layout: crosses the Grand Canal at its narrowest point
shops on both sides; central portico for the traffic of goods
turned to allow tall masts through the central arch
entries.found: Venice, Italy (Grand Canal)
entries.notes: Antonio da Ponte won the 1588 competition against Palladio and Michelangelo; the foundation piles were driven into the lagoon mud as for every Venetian palace.

entries.name: Charles Bridge (Karlův most)
materials: lime mortar (legendarily mixed with egg white, milk and whey)
entries.purpose: royal road crossing of the Vltava between Prague Castle and the Old Town
parts: two Gothic bridge towers (Old Town and Lesser Town)
layout: from Prague Castle across the Vltava to the Old Town
Old Town tower had two viewing levels; lesser tower gate opens to Malá Strana
statues were added over the 17th-18th centuries as votive offerings
entries.found: Prague, Czech Republic
entries.notes: Begun by Charles IV in 1357; replaced the Judith Bridge (1158-1172), destroyed by flood in 1342. The saint John of Nepomuk statue is the most kissed one.

entries.name: Stari Most (Mostar)
entries.purpose: foot crossing of the Neretva gorge linking Mostar's two Ottoman halves
parts: single stone arch span of 29 m
layout: spans the Neretva between the two fortified abutments
arch crown 24 m above the river
rebuilt using some original stones recovered from the riverbed
entries.found: Mostar, Bosnia and Herzegovina
entries.notes: Designed by Mimar Hayruddin for Sultan Süleyman the Magnificent; blown up by Croat forces on 9 Nov 1993. UNESCO World Heritage (2005).

entries.name: Victoria Falls Bridge
entries.purpose: rail and road crossing of the Zambezi below the Falls, on the imperial route from Cape to Cairo
parts: single steel arch span of 156.8 m
rail track and single carriageway with footpath
layout: crosses the gorge at right angles, about 450 m downstream of the falls
arch founded on cliff-edge piers; no piers in the river
viewing tours walk the arch; daredevils bungee and walk it on a plank
entries.found: on the border of Zambia and Zimbabwe at Victoria Falls
entries.notes: Ralph Freeman designed it; opened by Lord Curzon in 1905. The prototype for the Sydney Harbour Bridge.

entries.name: Zhaozhou Bridge (Anji Bridge)
entries.purpose: road bridge over the Xiao River on the imperial southern highway
parts: single open-spandrel stone segmental arch of 37.4 m
28 small spandrel arches to lighten the load and pass flood water
layout: single arch spanning the Xiao River without intermediate piers
open spandrels cut the weight and let floods through safely
survived earthquakes, wars and floods for 1,400 years
entries.found: Zhao County, Hebei Province, China
entries.notes: Oldest surviving open-spandrel stone arch bridge; architect Li Chun. Segmental stone arches 1,300 years before Europe's equivalents.

entries.name: Wooden covered bridge
materials: timber truss (Town lattice, Howe, Burr arch)
entries.purpose: roof keeps the truss dry; a wet wooden truss rots
layout: roof runs the full span; siding protects the joints
Town lattice truss used no iron, ideal for remote sites
single lane; weight limits posted or assumed
entries.found: New England, Pennsylvania, the upper Midwest; similar traditions in Switzerland and Germany
entries.notes: The US built roughly 10,000-15,000; about 700 survive. Cornish-Windsor Covered Bridge (1866) at 137 m is the longest historic US example.

entries.name: Bailey bridge
materials: prefabricated steel panels pinned by hand
entries.purpose: military and emergency span erected without cranes or special equipment
parts: rollers and launching nose for the build
layout: panels pin together with hand tools; a 30 m Class-40 span assembles in hours
single, double or triple trusses deepen the capacity
launched from one bank with a nose, then dropped into place
entries.found: WWII front lines, Korea, Vietnam, Afghanistan; disaster relief worldwide
entries.notes: Donald Bailey, a British civil servant, patented it in 1941. Some Bailey bridges erected after the 2015 Nepal earthquake carried traffic for decades.

entries.name: Millau Viaduct
entries.purpose: A75 autoroute crossing of the Tarn valley; removes a year-round traffic bottleneck
parts: seven concrete piers up to 245 m tall
steel masts rise above the deck to 343 m
six main spans of 342 m each
highest bridge piers in the world
layout: between Clermont-Ferrand and Béziers, passing over the Tarn and the Tarn valley
deck 270 m above the valley floor
masts are thinner than the Eiffel Tower at its base
entries.found: Millau, Aveyron, France
entries.notes: Designed by Norman Foster and Michel Virlogeux; opened December 2004. Still the tallest bridge in the world (mast 343 m).

entries.name: Duge Bridge (Beipanjiang)
entries.purpose: G56 Hangzhou-Ruili Expressway over the Beipan River gorge
parts: deck 565 m above the Beipan River
layout: crosses the gorge between Liupanshui and Xuanwei
world's highest bridge deck from 2016 to 2025 (overtaken by the Huajiang Grand Canyon Bridge, 625 m)
entries.found: Duge, on the Guizhou-Yunnan border, China
entries.notes: 565 m above the gorge. Reduced the Liupanshui-Xuanwei drive from hours to minutes; a defining monument of China's highway programme.

entries.name: Natural Bridge
entries.purpose: limestone arch cut by Cedar Creek; a landmark crossing and sacred site
parts: tunnel-like natural arch 65 m high and 27 m wide
layout: the creek cut through a limestone ridge, leaving the arch as a roof
arch thickens at the crown; walls taper inward
Virginia acquired it in 2015 as a state park
entries.found: Rockbridge County, Virginia, USA
entries.notes: George Washington surveyed it in 1750; sacred to the Monacan Nation. Formed over millions of years by Cedar Creek dissolving the limestone.

entries.name: Single log footbridge
entries.purpose: foot crossing of narrow streams and ravines
parts: notches or lashings at both ends
layout: one trunk felled across the gap, ends set into the banks
bark strips or adzed flat for footing
replaced when it rots or falls
entries.found: tropical forests (Borneo, Congo Basin), Appalachian and Scandinavian backlands
entries.notes: The simplest bridge a human can build: one tree, one gap. Living root bridges in Meghalaya are the self-repairing living version of the same idea.

entries.name: Living root bridge (Meghalaya)
entries.era: unknown; centuries old, some still growing
materials: living rubber fig (Ficus elastica) aerial roots
areca nut trunks as training guides
entries.purpose: community foot crossing of monsoon streams, self-building and self-repairing
parts: two or more rubber figs planted on opposite banks
roots trained and woven into a deck and rails
betel nut/palm guides replaced as roots take over
layout: figs planted on each bank; aerial roots tied together until they fuse
the bridge thickens as the trees grow; 10-15 years to bear weight, decades more to mature
must be regrown, not repaired: dead roots are replaced by live ones
entries.found: Mawlynnong, Pynursla, Nongriat and surrounding Khasi hills, Meghalaya, India
entries.notes: A living bridge strengthens with age and can outlast any timber span; monsoon floods only feed it. Some double-decker examples are 60+ years old.
